SUMMARY

Colgate-Palmolive Company(CL+2.23%)reported third quarter results featuring broad-based organic sales growth across four of its five divisions and all four product categories. Management reported that the company's productivity initiatives, specifically the "funding-the-growth" and "Strategic Growth and Productivity Program," effectively mitigated a 300 basis point headwind from material inflation. The company is increasing its advertising investment and focusing on premium innovation to sustain momentum, particularly in international markets. Management also reported a restructuring of the North American go-to-market model to transition from a channel-based structure to one focused on digital, social, and data connections. While emerging markets and the Hill's Pet Nutrition segment remained growth drivers, management acknowledged ongoing consumer uncertainty and cost volatility as key focus areas for the final quarter of the year.

Full Conference Call Transcript

Operator:Good morning, and welcome to today's Colgate-Palmolive 2026 third quarter conference call. This call is being recorded and is being simulcast live at www.colgatepalmolive.com. Now for opening remarks, I would like to turn this call over to Executive Vice President, Investor Relations, Claire Ross. Please go ahead.

Claire Ross:Good morning, and welcome to our Third Quarter 2026 Earnings Release Conference Call. This is Claire Ross, Executive Vice President, Investor Relations. Today's conference call will include forward-looking statements. Actual results could differ materially from these statements. Forward-looking statements inherently involve risks and uncertainties and are made on the basis of our views and assumptions at this time. Please refer to the third quarter earnings press release and our most recent filings with the SEC, including our 2025 annual report on Form 10-K and our subsequent SEC filings, all available on our website, for a discussion of the factors that could cause actual results to differ materially from these statements.

These remarks also include a discussion of non-GAAP financial measures, which exclude certain items from reported results, including these identified in tables four, six, seven, eight, and nine on the third quarter earnings press release. A full reconciliation to the corresponding GAAP financial measures and related definitions are included in the earnings press release. Joining me on the call this morning are Noel Wallace, Chairman, President, and Chief Executive Officer, and Stan Sutula, Chief Financial Officer. Noel will provide you with his thoughts on our results and our 2026 outlook. We will then open it up for Q&A.

Noel Wallace:Thanks, Claire, and good morning, everyone. A few thoughts. We are clearly pleased to have delivered another quarter of solid top and bottom line growth, particularly in the context of the continued global volatility we are seeing. Our strong results were broad-based, with organic sales growth in all four of our categories and four of our five divisions. We delivered solid gross margin expansion in a challenging cost environment. Base business EPS came in ahead of our expectations, even as we continue to increase our advertising. We are driving operating leverage through our productivity programs, including funding-the-growth and the Strategic Growth and Productivity Program, which drove lower costs.

Our balance sheet and cash flow performed through the third quarter was also very strong, with free cash flow up 7%, and we have returned $2.2 billion to shareholders year-to-date. Our strong on-the-ground execution, coupled with our continued investment in our AI capabilities, helped drive our performance. As was the case last quarter, sales growth was led by emerging markets, which were up mid-single digits, driven by India, Brazil, and China. We also had strong contributions from our European markets, where science-based premium innovation and our omni-channel demand generation model have led to record market shares. Our Hill's business had a very strong quarter across both therapeutic and wellness businesses.

We are pleased with our global momentum, but remain focused on executing our U.S. turnaround. As mentioned in the prepared remarks, we have seen market share improvements in toothpaste, but remain focused on driving the long-term reset, which starts with scaling premium innovation while reinforcing our core brands. We plan to increase both the pace and impact of innovation, with a pipeline focused on premium opportunities that can grow at scale. We are also strengthening our marketing model and support behind our core equities, with a sharper focus on high-priority channels, including digital, social, and emerging agentic commerce. Faster innovation, better use of AI and data, and more consistent execution will underpin that work.

On a global basis, we continue to invest in our revenue growth management strategies, as well as our omni-channel demand generation. We are scaling our AI capabilities globally with PromoAI now in many key markets, as well as with our proprietary AI innovation platform that has made our new product ideation process significantly faster than before. This leaves us well-positioned to deliver perceivable superior products to accelerate category growth and drive continued market share improvement.

We believe our efforts in RGM, AI, and our funding-the-growth initiatives give us the flexibility needed to invest appropriately in advertising to build our brands while driving profit and compounding EPS growth, even in a period of significant cost inflation, which we expect to remain elevated in the near term. We are also focused on delivering against our SGPP program, which is helping us build a simpler, more agile organization. The goal is not simply to manage through volatility. It is to emerge with a stronger business and an even more resilient business moving forward.

We are pleased with our year-to-date results, and while there are still some uncertainties ahead, we are optimistic that the strength of our global model will set us up for long-term success. With that, let me take your questions.

Operator:We will now begin the question-and-answer session. To ask a question, you may press star then one on your touch-tone phone. To withdraw your question, please press star then two. Please limit yourself to one question. If you have further questions, you may re-enter the question queue. Once again, if you would like to ask a question, please press star then one. Our first question will come from Peter Galbo of Bank of America. Please go ahead.

Peter Galbo:Hey, good morning. Thanks for taking the question. Noel, I noticed just in the prepared remarks, there was very little, if at all, commentary on 2027, and I know you're probably going through the planning process of that now. But maybe you could just give us some of the knowables for next year and some of the early puts and takes, particularly on the cost side. Clearly, you're delivering organic sales in line with plan, but I think there's just some concern around what the elevated cost environment might mean for next year. Just any early thoughts would be appreciated. Thanks very much.

Noel Wallace:Yeah, thanks, Peter. Clearly, since we're in 2026, we won't be sharing guidance on 2027 until the first quarter of next year. But clearly, the business model we're executing right now is helping to offset a very stubborn cost environment that we're experiencing around the world. As we said, as I said in my prepared remarks, we expect the cost environment to continue through the fourth quarter and into the early part of next year. We're focused on the levers we can control and executing our strategy in an environment where costs are clearly elevated. As we mentioned, tariffs would peak in the fourth quarter.

FX is moving a little bit against us, but we have the levers and the flexibility, and we believe the growth opportunities to continue to accelerate as we see the opportunities come to bear. We'll provide guidance on 2027 in the first quarter of next year. Right now, we're focused on what we can control and delivering against that as well as we can.

Operator:The next question comes from Dara Mohsenian of Morgan Stanley. Please go ahead.

Dara Mohsenian:Hey, good morning.

Noel Wallace:Morning, Dara.

Stan Sutula:Morning, Dara.

Dara Mohsenian:Just wanted to continue along that line of questioning. Can you give us a bit more specifics on what drove the gross margin upside in the quarter and the confidence on raising full-year gross margin guidance? Strong internal performance, that is a bit incongruous with a worse-than-expected external cost environment. Just wondering what really drove that internally and what was better than expected. Then, Noel, you mentioned some of the offsets you are focused on going forward. Maybe you can just touch on high level, the pricing lever, number one. Then second, on ad spend, you have had a 40% increase over a four-year period, with Q4 left to go, but it looks like about 40%. Huge increase over time.

Can you just talk about the ROI behind that, and if you are comfortable you are getting a strong ROI, and maybe if that is changing at all with some of these AI tech tools?

Noel Wallace:Thanks, Dara. I will let Stan talk in a minute about the cost environment, how we are dealing with that. A lot of the key initiatives that we have talked about, whether it is funding-the-growth, SG&A, have been a key driver of us helping to offset that. Let me talk to something that has been pretty consistent in our narrative over the last couple quarters, and that is our ability to get ahead of costing with pricing. If you go back to the first quarter of this year, we generated 220 basis points of pricing, 160 in the second quarter, and 200 more or less in the third quarter.

Clearly, we are getting pricing into the P&L as quickly as we can. Our general managers are using that to obviously drive some margin and help offset the uncertainty and the continued volatility we are seeing around cost. It is imperative that we get that pricing into the P&L upfront, as we see a continued challenging cost environment as well as potentially a challenging foreign exchange environment.

The second aspect of that is, certainly outside the U.S., we have been extremely successful in premiumizing our portfolio and driving more premium innovation, whether that is at Hill's with a very strong therapeutic business this quarter, whether that is through some of the Optic White success and the total relaunch we have had around the world. That premium innovation is clearly driving a nice upside in margin. The third is clearly the strong volume that we are consistently delivering through the P&L and the leverage we are getting at our manufacturing facilities with that volume. That is certainly helping to offset that.

With that, let me let Stan talk a little bit about the cost environment, what we are seeing, and how we are dealing with it with a couple initiatives we have in place.

Stan Sutula:Thanks, Noel. Let us start with the gross profit here. We are pleased with the gross profit performance on a year-to-date basis. As we look at that year-to-date performance, I think it is indicative of the comments Noel just made, but in particular, the expansion, if you kind of go down through the drivers, obviously material cost is a headwind. Material prices were roughly 300 basis points of a headwind in line with our expectations, but it remains a volatile environment around commodities, particularly around oil-based commodities. Helping to offset that was our productivity.

So, funding-the-growth drove over 290 basis points of offset to the material inflation, and that is really the hard work of all of the Colgate people around the world driving that performance. Pricing, as Noel just talked about, contributed 80 basis points of favorable, driven by RGM, and we had slight favorable from mix of about 20 basis points. As you kind of look, we guided for margin to be up on a year-on-year basis, up from roughly flat previously, and that is really driven by the performance we have, the confidence in our productivity as we exit the year, even though commodities are elevated.

Our commodities right now are largely locked in for Q4, so as we look at the overall balance, we think we can expand our gross profit margin for the year. Let me peel that back a little bit on raw materials. Raw materials and freight and logistics, I will lump that in, continues to operate in a really volatile environment. While we raised our guidance, raw and pack costs remained a significant headwind in Q3, particularly resins and petrochemicals, as well as pulp and paper. Our productivity, and that is funding-the-growth and SGPP, helped us to mitigate that within the quarter. We expect that underlying cost commodity pressure to remain elevated in Q4 and the near term.

Resins and petrochemicals remain high, but our cost projections for the balance of 2026 are largely locked in and included in our guidance. It will be, as you see the commodity volatility, I think a headwind heading into 2027. Freight logistics, we have all seen the escalating fuel costs, and those are having a direct impact on freight costs. As you know, those hit the P&L faster than commodity costs, which flow through inventory. Logistics costs have increased, they remain elevated, and our guidance for Q4 has the highest logistics cost quarter of the year, both in dollars and as a percent of sales. We expect that continued pressure through the end of the year and heading into next year.

Overall, it is the balance of our portfolio. It is the balance of offsetting those elevated costs through pricing, productivity, both from funding-the-growth and SGPP, that give us confidence to raise the guidance for the year.

Noel Wallace:Yeah, thanks, Stan. Just perhaps one additional clarification. We had an insignificant amount of tariff refund come through in the third quarter, so that was not the driver there, and we are not anticipating in the fourth quarter to have any further tariff refunds. Let me come back to your last part of your question, Dara, which was on advertising. Clearly, the strategy that we have been deploying for the last few years is to drive consistent top-line growth with the accelerated advertising spend that we are deploying around the world, and clearly, that model seems to be working for us.

We are spending a significant amount of time with understanding ROI, as I have talked about, and we feel very good about the ROIs that we are seeing. Now, the focus moving forward is to continue to accelerate advertising, but we are going to continue to use the tools we have at our disposal to optimize that spending as efficiently as possible. We have got a good handle of what is going on with the advertising line. We feel very good about the spend, and you see that playing out in the market share growth across the world. This quarter, on oral care, toothpaste up, toothbrushes up, mouthwash up.

All, we think, consistent with the innovation strategy and the brand building that we have. If we talk about some of the sluggishness that we have seen in categories around the world, it is also important that we continue as leaders in the category to support the growth with value-oriented premiumization to accelerate the advertising, excuse me, the category growth as we move forward.

Operator:The next question comes from Peter Grom of UBS. Please go ahead.

Peter Grom:Great. Thank you. Good morning, everyone. Hope you are doing well. I wanted to pivot to top line and maybe with an emphasis on Hill's. A very impressive organic sales growth this quarter. Can you maybe just unpack how the quarter came in relative to your expectations, what you are seeing from a category and market share standpoint, and how you see growth evolving from here? Thanks.

Noel Wallace:Yeah, thanks, and good morning, Peter. Hill's had a terrific quarter, probably above our expectations, but that team is pretty consistent in delivering against that, which is great to see. A lot of things happened in the quarter that were quite interesting. Clearly, the top line was good, 6.5% ex-private label. As we talked about, the category is still relatively sluggish. We're not seeing any material moves that we've talked about, at least through the first nine months of the year. Most of that growth is the strategic focus we have on growing segments, particularly cat and wet, and market share growth.

It's pleasing to see the fact that in a tough environment with increased competition, we're seeing good market share growth and very much the deliberate efforts we're placing in country category combinations and the segment growth opportunities that we're seeing, we're seeing good return on that investment. Therapeutic, as I mentioned earlier, had an excellent quarter. Prescription Diet dog was up behind mid-single digits. Prescription Diet cat was up double digits. Clearly, the therapeutic side of the business and the advocacy we're driving through the profession is playing out on the prescription side, and that's having a halo effect, obviously, on the rest of the business.

The other piece I'd call out is, we've been on this long-term journey to truly optimize our manufacturing and capacity that we have around the world, and the increased capacity we put in the wet is certainly delivering some of the improvements we're seeing there. But overall, with the strong volume growth we had in the quarter and the continued pricing, we saw gross margin up 170 basis points.

That's allowing us back to maybe dovetail some of the comments I made to Dara's question, to continue to accelerate the advertising spend on Hill's, because the ROI is absolutely there for us, and we're very happy with the campaign we're deploying, with the innovation that we're bringing across both Prescription Diet as well as the wellness side of the business. Overall, doing quite well. But it's a challenge category, and we need to continue to execute well to drive that consistent growth moving forward.

Operator:The next question comes from Lauren Lieberman of Barclays. Please go ahead.

Lauren Lieberman:Great. Thanks. Good morning. One thing that jumps out at me this morning was the overhead efficiencies, 90 basis points in SG&A, and that was, it has been growing each quarter of the year, sort of benefit. Just curious, how much of it is from the SGPP versus kind of ongoing productivity initiatives? How has, I guess, what you are doing internally allowed that productivity, the SG&A line, to become a bigger component of the P&L? Should we think of this as a new run rate? What is the forward look on SG&A efficiencies? Thanks.

Stan Sutula:Yeah, thanks, Lauren. I will take that one. On overhead efficiencies, it is really a combination of underlying productivity, but our Strategic Growth and Productivity Program has certainly been a driver. The teams have done a very nice job to implement that. Remember, when we looked at this, we are going to use the proceeds from that in two forms. We are going to invest back into the business, that is in things like advertising, like skillsets, AI, data, and analytics, and we are going to take some of that to the bottom line. There are still escalations underneath the covers as we are doing merit increases, and those vary around the world.

We are investing back in the business, but under the covers, even with that 90-point improvement, there is a lot of activity going on. SGPP, as a reminder, goes out through the end of 2028, so we have more that will be coming, and we have talked about that in the past. There is a nice mix here of underlying productivity plus the SGPP contributing to that. This is part of our business model that we are looking at, trying to drive margin improvement, manage overheads, grow the business to invest back in the underlying business, and deliver compounding profitable growth.

Operator:The next question comes from Steve Powers of Deutsche Bank. Please go ahead.

Steve Powers:Thank you. Good morning. Latin America remains a very solid growth driver, but as you called out in the prepared remarks, Mexico slowed this quarter, and there have been some external questions on forward momentum in Brazil. Maybe just an update on the puts and takes as you look around the region, and how you feel your business is positioned as we exit 2026 and move into 2027. Thank you.

Noel Wallace:Yeah, thanks, Steve, and good morning. Yeah, as you said, another solid quarter for Latin America, up 6%, which is pleasing, given some of the economic and political changes that we've seen across the region. But that's a testament to the team that we have in place and their ability to be highly resilient and agile as they adjust to things across the region. I think what's particularly pleasing is to see the strong volume growth in Latin America as well, so up 3.9%, and delivering that with 2% pricing in a tough environment. I'll get to both Brazil and Mexico in order.

Brazil, obviously up double digits, another very strong quarter, nice market share acceleration, largely driven by, I think, the strong advertising support, but importantly, the portfolio and focus we're putting on premiumizing oral care, with shares up there, driving execution in some of the faster-growing categories like shower gels and others, and doing a nice job executing broadly across the portfolio. We feel pretty good about where things are going. We'll need to watch the real carefully here, as you've seen it inch up or inch down, so to speak, as the dollar's appreciated against that currency quite considerably over the last week or two post the elections, and we hopefully will see that settle down here soon.

Mexico was hit with a difficult consumer backdrop, obviously some uncertainty in the categories of which we compete, but also some very specific retailer challenges that we had in the quarter. We will see some of those challenges start to subside as we exit the fourth quarter, and we feel comfortable that those will be behind us as we move into 2027, but we need to get those behind us. Executionally, we have got a really strong plan for next year, so I feel good about that, and the slowness in the quarter hopefully will be resurrected a bit as we move into the fourth quarter.

As I mentioned, we are anticipating another tough quarter in Mexico, but the rest of Latin America doing well. I would also call out Andina and Central America, good regions for us. Both had very positive organic growth and executing very well against that. As I look at some of the categories, we had strong category growth across Latin America in oral care, with double digits up in oral care, with low single to mid-single-digit growth in home care, and a slight decline in personal care. Broad-based, the personal care was driven somewhat by a softer shampoo business in Mexico specifically.

Across the board, oral care up very strongly, and home care up as well, so we are really pleased with that. The other thing I would say is shares. Shares were up across on oral care, both for toothpaste, toothbrushes, and mouthwash in the quarter. Again, we think across the board, executing well with the diversity of opportunities we have in Latin America. Brazil will continue to perform well. We need to get Mexico back on track, and that is some challenges that we are facing and dealing with, and the consumer hopefully will be a little bit more resilient as we move into a more settled environment potentially in 2027.

Operator:The next question comes from Filippo Falorni of Citi. Please go ahead.

Filippo Falorni:Hi. Good morning, everyone.

Stan Sutula:Morning, Filippo.

Noel Wallace:Morning, Filippo.

Filippo Falorni:Morning. I wanted to ask on the U.S. business. You mentioned in the prepared remarks that you are seeing some early signs of improvement in U.S. toothpaste. Noel, can you expand a bit on what parts of your plan are starting to work, what more you have to do there in terms of seeing further improvement? And just bigger picture, what you are seeing from a category standpoint in the U.S. Obviously, there has been a lot of focus on price and promotional activities. Do you see an environment of potentially seeing more pricing in your categories as we enter into next year, given the cost pressure that we talked already about early in the call? Thank you.

Noel Wallace:Yeah. Thanks, Filippo. Let me take the last part of your question first, because it's more holistically across the world. The one thing to bear in mind is the escalating cost environment that we're seeing impacts everyone, right? My expectation is that you'll have to see some pricing, as you've heard from others, go back into the business, and that will be executed differently by different brands and different competitors. There'll have to be some pricing to offset some of the raw material and logistics headwinds that everyone is faced with.

We are pleased, obviously, that we got pricing pretty broad-based in the quarter, as we've done in the second and first in the business, which, as I mentioned earlier, is critically important to maintain that gross margin and spending. A little bit more specifically on North America, our focus is on repowering our marketing model, really across the board, particularly focused on premium innovation. At the same time, we've got big core equities that we need to continue to support. We're going to be increasing over the next couple quarters the pace and impact of our innovation, and with a pipeline more specifically focused on premium opportunities, which is where the growth in the categories is coming from.

We're going to step up omni-demand, which has been a big focus structurally, and I'll talk about that maybe in just a second. Supporting our core equities with omni-channel demand generation, supporting the new premium innovation we're bringing into the market, and making sure that we're more deliberate and intentional about the priority growth channels that we're seeing across the U.S., whether that's digital, agentic, and an emerging social commerce business as well. Capabilities will be critical to invest in the capabilities in that organization, and we're very much in the process of seeing that now, very much work in process. That is the innovation resources to deliver breadth and quality moving forward.

We're stepping up our AI and data deployment with a series of multiple verticals in different parts of the organization, stronger execution fundamentals across different channels. Importantly, let me spend a minute talking about our go-to-market structure, which is clearly an area of opportunity for us in North America. Structurally, we built our go-to-market for a world of channels, and what we're seeing today is a world that runs on connections. Connections with data, connections with retailers, connections with different platforms that ultimately get to the consumer. We're restructuring to win that connection so we get more premium innovation that earns its full value with the consumer.

That premium innovation, in terms of how we're structuring our commercial teams on the ground, is continuing to be optimized because we think we can execute more effectively moving forward, particularly with the increased advertising we're putting into that region. You mentioned categories. Categories maybe improved a bit as we exited the quarter, but still relatively sluggish. But overall, they're more or less where they've been through the first half of the year, and anticipate that as we get a strong innovation cycle in 2027 coming in, that we'll see those categories and through some a little bit more pricing start to inflect more positively moving forward.

Operator:The next question comes from Bonnie Herzog of Goldman Sachs. Please go ahead.

Bonnie Herzog:All right. Thank you. Good morning, everyone. I had a question on consumption trends across your markets, with gas prices still elevated. Curious to hear from you if you've seen any further deterioration in consumption across your markets, or has it been more of the same? Then, would love to hear which markets are doing well and maybe which ones have been more pressured recently. Then lastly, what is your expectation for category growth for the rest of this year and then for next year? Does the guidance assume sequential improvement in trends over the course of the year? Thanks.

Noel Wallace:Yeah. Good morning. Thank you, Bonnie. So, there's a lot there. Let me start, I guess, big picture, category growth overall globally. We're seeing growth in the 1.5%-3% globally, with obviously emerging markets driving a faster growth in that 3%-5% range, and the developed markets driving growth in that 1.5%-2% range. So, overall, 1.5%-3% globally, with emergings at the higher end, 3%-5%. And the expectation is that will continue. Now, that being said, there'll be some probably more pricing that needs to be taken globally that will take that up. A lot more premium innovation, because that's where the growth is in the categories across the board, so we'll see that come into it.

But we're going to watch that very carefully. Our focus on the increased support and the increased premiumization is intended to obviously grow our retailers' categories. Let me walk around the world. I guess I will start with emerging markets, which are up mid-single digits. Asia had a really good quarter, although I would say the China business continued to be challenged from a category standpoint. It has not really changed from what we have seen over the last 9 months. India, still pretty good. We had obviously another really strong quarter in India with double digits, and that was really driven by a lot of the premium innovation that we are seeing.

In terms of our China business, pleased that Greater China was up mid-single digits, and high single digits for the Colgate part of the business, and low single digits for Hawley & Hazel, as we exited the quarter. The category is still somewhat challenged. You are seeing brick and mortar very, very soft, and a significant migration continues to the online part of the business, particularly in more social-driven platforms like Douyin. Latin America, obviously, as I mentioned just earlier, I will not get into more detail there. Another strong quarter.

Categories pretty much consistent, maybe inflected a little bit positive towards the end of the quarter, particularly in Brazil, maybe a little softer in Mexico, as I mentioned, but good numbers in Central America and Andina. EMEA on the emerging side, overall, the African markets continue to perform well. We had some blips in the Middle East with some pricing challenges there. But overall, EMEA from an emerging market standpoint is performing quite well from a category standpoint. Flipping over to the developed part of the world, categories, as I mentioned, in that 1.5 to more or less 2.5 growth rate.

North America is where we are seeing the most pressure, but a little bit of improvement as we exited the quarter. Europe categories remain roughly flat. No big change there in the second quarter and the third quarter from what we have seen. However, we continue to drive really nice market share on the premium side of the business, particularly in Southern and Northern Europe, where we saw nice growth as well. Hill's, as I mentioned just now, the category remains somewhat subdued, but we are seeing nice growth in certain segments. So, in segments particularly where we are under-indexed, like cat, like wet, and we are generating very nice growth against that.

That is more or less how I characterize the consumption around the world, and clearly, I think we will see that continued trend in the fourth quarter, and we will talk about 2027 when we get there.

Operator:The next question comes from Olivia Tong of Raymond James. Please go ahead.

Olivia Tong:Great. Thanks. One more follow-up on Hill's, given the strong volume-led acceleration. Can you talk about the sustainability of that and whether you are seeing more distribution with recent innovations? You call that therapeutic and cats. Obviously, those are still the biggest growth drivers, but are the growth drivers widening, or is that still the lion's share of the growth? Then just on margins, a bit surprising that you saw a decline given the sales upside.

I know it is a small decline, but given the sales upside, obviously overall strength of margins for Colgate as a whole, can you talk about the drivers there and whether it is investment levels behind new innovation or marketing, or what needs to happen to get better operating leverage on pretty strong top-line results? Thank you.

Noel Wallace:Yeah. Good morning, Olivia. Thank you. So again, the strategy that we are executing against Hill's, perhaps very redundantly boring because it is working for us, and we clearly see growth opportunities in the growing segments, and we are executing against those really well. So the wet business was up really, really nicely. The cat business was up really, really nicely, both across Prescription Diet and Science Diet. Just to give you a couple facts there. Science Diet cat on the wellness side was up high single digits. Science Diet, Prescription Diet was up double digits. So clearly, we are growing in the growth segments. Likewise, very similar trends on Science Diet wet as well as Prescription Diet wet.

So we are focused on those opportunities where we see real upside, despite the fact that some of the other parts of the business, particularly dog dry, is relatively flat to down, and we are seeing that migration to smaller pets, and we are capitalizing on the strategies to do that. Our online business continues to perform very well, and we still continue to be able to execute against those initiatives there. The other aspect moving forward, we have not necessarily talked about it, is Fresh. Now, Fresh was insignificant in the quarter.

As I have talked about in previous meetings, we announced the launch of our Single Protein diets in late June, with three diets, chicken and brown rice, beef and carrot, and lamb and pumpkin, making everyone hungry here, I am sure. But the key is that we are in a very deliberate and methodical rollout of that. We are doing it very carefully. We're trying to ensure that the quality that we bring to the vets and the reputation that we have behind the Hill's brand name is executed and consistent with where we want that business to be long-term. We're looking to drive this business in a way that we create long-term sustainable growth for the business.

It's a disciplined rollout, and we'll see that continue to roll out as we move through the balance of this year and into 2027. I would say that the Prime launch in Australia, the Prime business in Australia, that team continues to execute exceptionally well with that business, and we're transferring those learnings over to us. On the margin side, I'll let Stan give you a couple more details on that.

Stan Sutula:Yeah. So, not clear if your question is on Hill's operating margin, which is down just slightly. That really represents these investments, the investments into advertising, growing the brand, the margin, and launching of Fresh, because on an operating basis for the total company, the EBIT margins are actually up slightly year-on-year. Again, we always look to balance the investment portfolio. So, our capital allocation remains the same. We're going to invest back in the business. It ties into why we launched the SGPP program, to invest back in the business as well as take to the bottom line.

You're going to see us make those investments in innovation, in functional capability, and Noel talked several times about how we're applying AI, and then in some day-to-day operational efficiencies in our manufacturing, in our advertising, and in new categories like Fresh launch in the U.S. So, we always balance those out, and again, we delivered bottom line EPS growth faster than top line organic.

Operator:The next question comes from Chris Carey of Wells Fargo Securities. Please go ahead.
